title: Showcase: one line of Python
summary: Run the week 11 badge in Python for the family, explain one real line of code, and say what comes next season.

figure.alt: The showcase layout: the micro:bit badge with its battery running next to a laptop screen showing the Python code, an arrow pointing from the badge toward the line being pointed at on screen. Text below lists the demo order: say it, show it, point at a line, say what's next.

items.s: say it, show it, point at a line, say what's next

steps.title: Run the Python badge
steps.body:
Set the badge up before the family is watching, so name scrolling, the heartbeat and the button A happy face are already working.

Run the demo:

1. Clip on the battery pack before anyone is watching.
2. Say what the badge does, before you do it.
3. Watch your name scroll, then let the heart beat a few times.
4. Press button A and show the happy face.
5. Open the Python code and point at one line you understand, like `while True:`, `sleep(500)`, or `if button_a.was_pressed():`.
6. Say in your own words what that line does and why it is there.
7. Say one sentence: what would you build next season, the badge, the robot, or something new.

If the board shows a scrolling error instead of your program, read the line number out loud to the family. Show them the exact word or missing colon at that line. That still counts as a real demo.

steps.title: Show it
steps.prompt: A photo of the badge running with the code on screen, or a short video of the whole demo, the pointed-at line and the error recovery if it happens.

extras.title: Point at two lines, not just one
extras.body:
Most demos only point at one line. Point at two, and connect them.

1. Before the family watches, open your Python code from week 11.
2. Pick a second line, different from the one you already planned to explain.
3. Write one sentence for what that second line does, in your own words.
4. Write one sentence for how the two lines work together.
5. During the demo, point at both lines and say both sentences out loud.

What to notice: most single lines of code only make sense next to another line.

extras.title: Say what happens next
extras.body:
If you kept building next season, what would you want your badge or robot to do?

Decide on one idea for something you would build next.

It must build on something real from this season, the badge, the dice, or the robot.
It must have one number you would want to choose by testing, even if unbuilt.
It must be said out loud to someone in your house, during or after the demo.

Sketch your idea on paper first.

How to know it works: someone else can repeat your idea back to you in their own words.

extras.title: The battery's push, one more time
extras.body:
Find out whether the same battery pack from week 4 still gives the same voltage now.

1. Predict first: guess how many volts the multimeter will read across the battery pack you used back in week 4. Write your number in the Maker's Log.
2. Set a multimeter to measure DC volts.
3. Touch the two probes to the battery pack's wires and read the number.
4. Write down today's number next to your week 4 number, if you saved it.

Compare: is today's number close to week 4's number, lower, or about the same?

Teach it: tell a grown-up in two sentences why a battery's push fades a little more with every week of use.

extras.title: Rewrite your best log
extras.body:
Your logs are the writing you do here, and writing gets better by rewriting, not by more of it. Pick your best log from this sprint and rewrite it once.

1. Read the log out loud. Mark every sentence that tries to say two things.
2. Rewrite so each sentence carries one idea. Split, do not shorten.
3. Find every adjective (hard, cool, weird) and replace it with a number or a fact: how many tries, how long, what broke.
4. Put the reason before the claim: "the loop ran twice, so the heart flashed twice" rather than "the heart flashed twice, because the loop ran twice".
5. Read both versions to someone and ask which one they could follow without you in the room.

What to notice: the rewrite is usually shorter and says more. That is the whole trick.
